notes: Simplified harmonic reference. Chord progressions are functional facts; sources are cited per entry. Do not treat as a transcription of any recording.

common.name: Axis progression
common.description: The four-chord pop loop; rotates through all four starting points.

common.name: Pop-punk rotation
common.description: The axis progression starting on the relative minor; common in pop-punk and modern pop.

common.name: 50s progression
common.description: Doo-wop changes also known as the Stand by Me progression.

common.name: Three-chord song
common.description: The basic three-chord vocabulary behind countless rock, folk and country songs.

common.name: I–IV–I–V
common.description: Open, anthemic alternation between tonic and subdominant, then dominant.

common.name: I–V–IV–I
common.description: Mixolydian-flavoured rock cadence with a strong return to the tonic.

common.name: I–bVII–IV
common.description: Classic rock move borrowing the flat seventh; often heard as a two-chord I–bVII vamp.

common.name: I–bVII–bVI–bVII
common.description: Descending flat-side rock loop with a strong modal colour.

common.name: Andalusian cadence
common.description: The Spanish/fandango descent, also common in rock and film music.

common.name: Minor pop loop
common.description: The minor-key version of the axis progression, common in modern pop and rock.

common.name: ii–V–I
common.description: The essential jazz cadence, usually played with seventh chords.

common.name: ii–bII7–I
common.description: Tritone substitution for the dominant; chromatic bass motion into the tonic.

common.name: I–vi–ii–V turnaround
common.description: Circle-of-fifths turnaround used to close a section and lead back to the top.

common.name: 12-bar blues
common.description: The twelve-bar form with dominant sevenths; the backbone of blues and early rock.

common.name: 8-bar blues
common.description: A compact eight-bar blues form, common in early blues and rock and roll.

common.name: I–V–IV–V
common.description: Dominant-heavy blues/rock loop; the V–IV motion gives it a raw, driving feel.

common.name: Royal road progression
common.description: The IV–V–iii–vi progression behind many Japanese pop and anime songs.

common.name: Pachelbel's Canon
common.description: The famous eight-chord descending sequence, endlessly reused in pop and film music.

common.name: I–IV–bVII–IV
common.description: Mixolydian rock progression with a whole-step descent from the tonic.

common.name: i–iv–V
common.description: Minor tonic and subdominant with a raised-leading-tone dominant; a classic minor cadence.
